_meta.description: Participant-facing hints controlled by the instructor. Each vuln can have a hint with a title, description, and enabled flag. When enabled=true, participants see the hint banner on pages where the vuln is active.

auth.g1.title: SQL Injection — Login Bypass
auth.g1.description: The Customer ID is concatenated into the login SQL query, so crafted input can change the query logic and bypass the password check. Goal: sign in as your own account without the password.

levels.subtitle: Level 0 · classic injection
steps: Your Customer ID goes straight into the SQL query. Type a single quote ' in it and submit — a database error confirms the input is injectable.
You do not need the password: comment out the rest of the query so only your Customer ID is checked. MySQL's line comment is -- followed by a space.
Use your own Customer ID, then ' -- with a trailing space, and any password: <yourID>' --

levels.subtitle: Level 1 · comments blocked
steps: The single quote still errors, so injection works — but comment tokens (--, #, /*) and UNION are now filtered out.
If you cannot comment the password check away, make the condition true for your row another way — a boolean OR is not blocked.
Close the string and OR in a always-true test; the query's own trailing quote balances yours: <yourID>' OR '1'='1

levels.subtitle: Level 2 · blind + brackets
steps: No error is shown now (blind). The query also wraps the ID check in parentheses, with the password check OUTSIDE the brackets.
A plain comment leaves an unbalanced ) and silently fails; a bare OR cannot get past the password check outside the parentheses. You must close the bracket first.
Close the parenthesis, then comment out the rest: <yourID>') -- (trailing space)

auth.l10.title: Brute-Force Attack (OTP)
auth.l10.description:
When a system uses short numeric codes (like OTPs) without rate limiting or lockout, an attacker can systematically try every possible combination. With only 10,000 possibilities and no throttle, automation discovers the code in seconds.
After SQLi login, use the brute-force script in the lab code panel to find the OTP. When successful, a flag modal automatically appears with your flag ready to copy.

auth.l11.title: OTP in Response Body (2FA Leak)
auth.l11.description: The 4-digit login OTP is exposed to the client instead of staying server-side, so you can recover it without the victim's phone. Look at the script /public/js/otp-validation.js.

levels.subtitle: Level 0 · plaintext
steps: The OTP is a second factor — it should only reach your phone. But the page may hand it to the browser. It is not in the HTML; look at the scripts the page loads.
Open DevTools → Network or Sources and inspect /public/js/otp-validation.js — it carries a per-session SESSION_DATA object.

The OTP is in plain text in the _otp field of SESSION_DATA, and the flag is right beside it in plain text in _flag. Read the OTP to log in and read the flag directly — at this level nothing is hidden.

levels.subtitle: Level 1 · predictable from a seed
steps: There is no _otp anymore — but SESSION_DATA leaks a _seed (the OTP token's id) and your _uid (user id). Why would the client need those?
The OTP is derived from those two values (same inputs → same OTP). In CTF the _algo field hints the formula.

OTP = first 8 hex chars of sha256(_seed + _uid) read as an integer, last 4 digits (i.e. % 10000). Concatenate _seed and _uid as strings (not numeric addition), SHA-256 it, take the first 8 hex chars, parseInt(hex, 16) % 10000, zero-pad to 4. (Full one-liner is in the vuln matrix.) Then decrypt the flag: it is sealed in _flag_enc (flag XOR sha256(OTP)) — unseal it with the OTP you recovered.

levels.subtitle: Level 2 · secrets in response headers
steps: The JS body has no OTP, no seed, no hash now — only breadcrumbs. Look where else a response can carry data: the HTTP response headers of /public/js/otp-validation.js (DevTools → Network → that request → Response Headers).
Two custom headers are set: X-Otp-Check (a sha256 of the OTP) and X-Flag-Enc (the sealed flag). A hash is one-way… but the OTP is only 4 digits — 10,000 possibilities.

Brute-force it: hash every code 0000–9999 with SHA-256 and compare to X-Otp-Check until it matches. (Full console snippet is in the vuln matrix — read headers via fetch(...).headers.get().) Then decrypt the flag: flag = base64decode(X-Flag-Enc) xor sha256(otp).

auth.l12.title: JWT Forgery (forge → access)
auth.l12.description: The app trusts a JWT carried in the browser-readable access_token cookie (or Authorization: Bearer). Forge one with role:admin to escalate without the signing key.

levels.subtitle: Level 0 · signature not verified
steps: A JWT has three base64url parts: header.payload.signature. The payload holds your role. The token is in the access_token cookie — decode it.
At this level the server only checks that a signature segment is present — it never verifies the HMAC. So you can change the payload and leave the signature as-is.
Set the payload to role:admin / sub:ADMIN001, re-encode, keep any signature string, and write it back as the access_token cookie. (Skeleton in the vuln matrix.)

levels.subtitle: Level 1 · alg:none
steps: Keeping the old signature no longer works — the HMAC is checked now. Look at the header's alg field instead.
If alg is none, the server treats the token as unsigned and skips signature verification entirely.
Header {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}, admin payload, empty signature (trailing dot). (Skeleton in the vuln matrix.)

levels.subtitle: Level 2 · case-sensitive alg check
steps: Plain alg:none is rejected now — but the reject check and the accept check don't agree on casing.
Only the exact lowercase none is blocked; a differently-cased value still reaches the unsigned-accept path.
Use {"alg":"None"} (or NONE) with an empty signature. (Skeleton in the vuln matrix.)

statements.l1.title: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)
statements.l1.description:
The server uses a client-supplied identifier to fetch records but does NOT verify that the requesting user owns that resource. Changing the identifier to another user's value exposes their data.
Modify the account_id parameter in the URL to access other users' statements. When you view an account that doesn't belong to you, a flag modal appears automatically.

transfer.l1.title: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)
transfer.l1.description:
Client-side restrictions (disabled fields, hidden inputs, readonly attributes) are cosmetic — they do NOT enforce security. The server must verify ownership on every request. Manipulate the 'from_account_number' field in the transfer form to transfer from another user's account.
When you successfully transfer from an account you don't own, a flag modal appears automatically.

statements.g2.title: SQL Injection (Data Extraction)
statements.g2.description: The Statements search box folds your term straight into a WHERE clause (remarks LIKE '%...%'), so a crafted term becomes SQL and can read other tables. Your flag is a per-user value stored only in the ctf_flags table (columns flag + username, where username is your Customer ID); the query returns 7 columns.

levels.subtitle: Level 0 · raw term (in-band & error-based)
steps: Use the Search (remarks) box on Statements. The term goes into ... remarks LIKE '%<you>%', so a single quote ends the string and the rest runs as SQL.
Confirm it is injectable: search x' AND '1'='1 (rows) versus x' AND '1'='2 (none). The query has 7 columns.

Dump in-band with UNION — put the flag in the Remarks column, because the Date column is truncated to 10 chars (it would show just BANKSPLOIT): %' UNION SELECT username,flag,3,4,5,6,7 FROM ctf_flags-- . Each row then shows a Customer ID (Date) and its flag (Remarks) — read the one matching your Customer ID.
Or error-based (raw SQL errors are shown at L0): x' AND extractvalue(1,concat(0x7e,(SELECT flag FROM ctf_flags WHERE username='<your id>')))-- — the flag appears inside the error message.
Submit your own flag in Flag Submission.

levels.subtitle: Level 1 · keyword blacklist (bypass the filter)
steps: A filter now strips union, select and the comment tokens -- # /* */ from the term — in a single pass — and SQL errors are hidden, so a plain ' UNION SELECT ... comes back empty and looks un-injectable.
The single pass is the flaw: nest the keyword so removing the inner word rebuilds it — UNIunionON, SELselectECT (empty inline comments uni/**/on work too).
Comments are stripped, so you cannot finish with -- ; balance the quote instead by ending the payload with ' OR '%'=' (or WHERE '%'=').
Full dump: %' UNIunionON SELselectECT username,flag,3,4,5,6,7 FROM ctf_flags WHERE '%'=' — Customer ID in the Date column, flag in Remarks, same as L0.
Submit your own flag.

levels.subtitle: Level 2 · UNION blocked (boolean-blind)
steps: Now union is stripped repeatedly (nesting cannot rebuild it) and errors are hidden — no in-band channel and no error channel. But AND, sub-selects and quotes still reach the query, so you read the flag one character at a time.
The oracle is “do my own rows come back?”: house%' AND 1=1-- returns rows (true), house%' AND 1=2-- returns none (false).

Extract char by char: house%' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT flag FROM ctf_flags WHERE username='<your id>'),1,1)='B'-- — rows mean the 1st character is B. Walk positions 1…23 across the charset (the flag looks like BANKSPLOIT{...}).
Automate it in practice — e.g. sqlmap --technique=B on the q parameter, or a short script. The flag never appears on screen; you reconstruct it.
Submit the reconstructed flag.

statements.g9.title: OS Command Injection
statements.g9.description:
When the application passes user-controlled input to a system shell command (via exec, system, passthru, etc.), shell metacharacters like semicolons or backticks can break out of the intended command and execute arbitrary OS commands on the server.
The flag is written to a file named flag_g9_*.txt

auth.l25.title: Session Puzzling (forgot-password takeover)
auth.l25.description: The forgot-password journey tracks progress in session state that is not bound to the user it was earned for, so recovery progress for one account can be reused to take over another.

levels.subtitle: Level 0 · auth key overloaded at step 1
steps: Open /forgot-password. The first step only asks for a Customer ID — no password, OTP or security questions yet.
Step 1 only asks for a Customer ID — submit one that is not yours.

Entering the Customer ID already writes a full authenticated session for that user, before any OTP or questions. Just browse to /dashboard — you are them. Capture the flag from the modal (you are signed in as the victim).

levels.subtitle: Level 1 · recovery stage carries across users
steps: The flow has four pages (Customer ID → OTP → questions → reset). Progress is stored in the session as recovery_stage, and the target account as recovery_uid.
Complete the whole flow for your own account (you know its OTP and answers) until you reach the Set a new password page — now recovery_stage = 2.
Open the first page /forgot-password in a new tab (same session) and submit a victim's Customer ID. It overwrites recovery_uid but leaves recovery_stage at 2.
Go to /forgot-password/reset — it now serves the victim's reset page with no OTP and no questions. Set their password to take over. The flag is keyed to your own account.

levels.subtitle: Level 2 · stale verification state
steps: Same shape as Level 1: reach the reset page legitimately with your own account, then swap in a victim's Customer ID on the step-1 page in another tab.
The earned recovery state is still not bound to the exact account that earned it, so the reset page opens for the swapped-in victim — drive it to /forgot-password/reset and set their password.
